body: South Korea uses various licence plates. Pre-2006 plates are short and green, while post-2006 plates are white for private cars and yellow for commercial vehicles.
Most South Korean coverage is Generation 3, often showing the back of a black, white, or silver Google car. A key characteristic is the complete lack of an antenna.
A significant portion of South Korean Street View coverage was filmed in autumn and winter. This results in many landscapes with sparse foliage, though spring and summer coverage also exists.
The Korean script, Hangul, is highly distinctive due to the presence of circles in many characters. This makes it easily distinguishable from other East Asian writing systems.
South Korean utility poles feature distinctive black and yellow diagonal stripes near the bottom. Unlike in Taiwan, these stripes do not reach the ground and are a brighter yellow.
Most utility poles in South Korea are topped with a tapered 'spike'.
South Korea drives on the right side of the road.
Roads in South Korea typically have yellow middle lines and white outer lines.
You can sometimes find red block markings painted on the roads.
Triangular warning signs have a yellow background. In contrast, circular prohibition signs and yield signs have a white background.
Street signs are typically blue, arrow-shaped, and often seen hanging from bars attached to utility poles.
Directional signs in South Korea are green with white text.
Pedestrian crossings are often painted with a yellow and white pattern.
South Korean pedestrian crossing signs are easily recognizable due to their distinct pentagonal shape and blue background.

Korean buildings feature very distinctive blue house numbers, often shaped like a literal house. They display the full address in both Hangul and Latin script, and unique designs can help with region-guessing.
South Korea uses black and white wedge-shaped bollards that have a round yellow reflector on the front.
The South Korean landscape is predominantly mountainous. It's rare to find a location where you can't see hills or mountains in the distance.
Red brick is a very common building material for buildings in South Korea.
Many buildings feature traditional tiled roofs with upward-curving sides and decorative corners. Blue roofs are also a very common sight.
Street View coverage in South Korea is quite limited and spotty. It is mainly concentrated on large highways and in and around major cities.
South Korean area codes generally increase as you go further south, starting from 02 in the north. Seoul is the only area with a two-digit area code (02).
Generation 2 coverage is almost exclusively found in Seoul and Busan, with most other instances having been updated to newer imagery.
A small camera mounted above the brake light of the Street View car is a specific meta for coverage northeast of Seoul and around Pohang.
Jeju is a volcanic island characterized by its dark volcanic soil. Volcanoes can often be seen in the distance.
The island of Jeju features many distinctive rock walls constructed from dark volcanic rocks.
The Gimje area is one of the only completely flat regions in South Korea. It is recognizable by its wide-open, yellow-green fields.
House numbers in the Hampyeong region are identifiable by the large white section at the top of the sign.
